title: Why the Far Right's War on Modern Architecture Matters
gist: Jan-Werner Mueller argues Germany's far-right AfD's focus on architecture and cultural policy is more significant than it appears, since cultural policy is one of the few areas the party can actually change at the state level and is tied to its exclusionary political agenda; he flags that the AfD's two-year polling surge and the Saxony-Anhalt state election could fatally undermine the political 'firewall' that has kept it from power. This is a paywalled teaser excerpt.

themes.theme: Cultural policy as a lever for the far right

insights.claim: The AfD's fixation on architecture is more revealing than it may seem, because cultural policy is one of the few areas where the party can actually change conditions on the ground at the state level, and it is intimately tied to the far right's exclusionary political agenda.
insights.speaker: Jan-Werner Mueller
insights.so_what: Frames a seemingly niche cultural fight (over modernist/Bauhaus architecture) as a substantive proxy indicator of the AfD's actual governing agenda and capacity where it holds regional power -- worth tracking as an early signal of policy implementation, not just polling.
insights.quote: The Alternative for Germany's fixation on architecture is more revealing than it may seem.

insights.claim: The AfD has been surging in the polls for two years but has been kept from power by other parties' refusal to enter governing coalitions with it -- a 'firewall' that depends on the AfD never winning outright majorities, and which the author suggests could be fatally undermined by the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
insights.speaker: Jan-Werner Mueller
insights.so_what: Flags a specific state election (Saxony-Anhalt) as a potential inflection point where the AfD could win an outright majority, breaking the coalition-exclusion norm that has so far kept it out of executive power in Germany.
